records.name: Deforestation & Land-Cover Change
records.question: Where has forest cover changed, and what land-cover classes replaced it?
records.summary: Compare land-cover dates, trace forest loss and summarize transitions into other land uses.
overview: The video follows land-cover changes between 1992 and 2022. It uses class metadata to translate raster codes into named land-cover categories, making changes easier to interpret.

After aligning the data, the analysis builds transition summaries and distinguishes forest-to-cropland change from other forest-loss pathways. Mapped classes and tabular exports keep the geography connected to the quantitative result.
inputs: Categorical land-cover rasters for the comparison dates
Class definitions and metadata
A study boundary and an area-calculation reference system
steps: Inspect the dates, class definitions and spatial alignment.
Identify forest classes and compare them with the later land-cover categories.
Calculate transitions and summarize their areas or proportions.
Map the different loss pathways and export the results.
outputs: Forest-loss maps separated by destination class
Land-cover transition summaries and exportable tables
review: Check that class definitions are comparable across dates.
Review alignment and area units before interpreting change totals.

records.name: Sea-Level Rise & Coastal Inundation
records.question: Which coastal areas connect to the ocean under a defined water-level scenario?
records.summary: Separate ocean-connected inundation from inland low points and prepare coastal exposure layers for review.
overview: This demonstration starts with elevation and hydrological information to examine sea-level-rise scenarios. Its central distinction is between land that is simply low and land connected to ocean-driven flooding.

The described sequence cleans waterbody inputs, applies hydrological masking and converts raster results into vector layers. Reprojection and GeoParquet export prepare the output for mapping and subsequent analysis.
inputs: Elevation data with known units and vertical reference
Waterbody and coastal-connectivity information
A study area and an explicit water-level scenario
steps: Inspect elevation, spatial references and the chosen scenario.
Prepare waterbody data and distinguish coastal connectivity from inland depressions.
Derive the scenario result and inspect the inundation boundaries.
Convert and export the mapped layers for further analysis.
outputs: Vector outputs suitable for maps and exposure summaries
review: Check elevation quality, vertical reference and connectivity assumptions.
Treat the result as a defined scenario, rather than a forecast of a particular storm.

records.name: Future Crop Suitability
records.question: How might suitable maize-growing areas shift under a future climate scenario?
records.summary: Connect current crop distribution with climate variables to compare present and future suitability in the US Corn Belt.
overview: This case study combines bioclimatic variables with crop-distribution information to model maize suitability. The description identifies WorldClim, NASA GFSAD and IFPRI SPAM among the inputs.

The trained model is applied to a future climate scenario, then compared with present conditions to map potential gains and losses. Those maps describe modeled suitability under the selected assumptions; they do not establish future yields.
inputs: Present and future bioclimatic variables
Crop extent or distribution data
A stated climate model, scenario, horizon and study area
steps: Align climate and crop data and prepare the sampling design.
Train and evaluate a suitability model against the available observations.
Apply the model to the selected future climate inputs.
Compare present and future rasters to locate suitability gains and losses.
review: Review sampling, validation and spatial transfer limitations.
Keep the selected climate scenario and time horizon attached to every result.

records.name: Sports Facility Site Selection
records.question: Where could new sports centers best serve Riyadh?
records.summary: Compare demand, access, competition and terrain to identify candidate development zones in Riyadh.
overview: The Riyadh demonstration combines several location factors in a common hexagonal grid. Demographics describe potential demand, while transport access, commercial activity and nearby competitors add context to each candidate area.

The video describes a suitability index built from normalized indicators, then groups high-scoring cells into development clusters. The result is a transparent shortlist for review, with individual indicators behind each score.
inputs: Population and demographic layers; nighttime-light data
Public services, transport stops, shopping malls and existing gyms
Building density, land cover and elevation
steps: Define the study area and organize the city into comparison cells.
Build indicators for demand, commercial activity, accessibility and competition.
Review land-cover and terrain constraints, then normalize the selected indicators.
Combine the indicators and examine the resulting high-scoring clusters.
outputs: Suitability map and candidate development clusters
Indicator values explaining each candidate score
review: Review how weights and thresholds affect the ranking.
Check that access, population and competitor data represent the same geography and relevant period.

records.name: Advanced Vector & Raster Analysis
records.question: How can vector and raster analysis work together in one reviewable GIS process?
records.summary: Explore one complete demonstration covering vector operations, satellite imagery, NDVI, coastline proximity and building-level elevation.
overview: This walkthrough brings building footprints, roads, census tracts, elevation and Sentinel-2 imagery into a single GIS demonstration. It shows how attribute inspection, spatial relationships and raster processing can be combined without treating each operation as a separate application.

The same video covers NDVI and false-color imagery, building distance to a coastline, and mean elevation within building footprints. These are different analytical tasks within the original demonstration, presented together here.
inputs: Building footprints, roads, census tracts and a coastline layer
A digital elevation model and Sentinel-2 imagery
Compatible coordinate systems, attribute definitions and a study boundary
steps: Explore the source attributes and prepare the vector and raster inputs.
Apply vector operations such as buffers, clipping, selection and spatial joins.
Inspect raster tasks including masking, NDVI, false-color composites and reclassification.
Review proximity and zonal-statistics outputs alongside the source layers.
outputs: Mapped vector and raster results from the combined demonstration
review: Check coordinate systems, raster alignment, distance and elevation units.
Review imagery dates, spectral bands, clouds and missing pixels.
Interpret proximity, terrain summaries and vegetation indices according to their individual methods.

records.name: Rooftop Solar Potential
records.question: Which building rooftops show stronger modeled solar potential?
records.summary: Combine surface elevation and building footprints to compare rooftop solar potential in Miami-Dade County.
overview: The demonstration aligns a USGS digital surface model with OpenStreetMap building footprints. Rooftops are isolated before modeling radiation with slope, orientation and shading effects.
Zonal summaries translate the modeled surface into building-level measures and potential classes. Monthly radiation patterns add a seasonal view alongside the overall comparison.
inputs: A digital surface model
Building footprints in an aligned coordinate system
A modeling year and solar-radiation parameters
steps: Check surface-model and building-footprint alignment.
Isolate rooftops and calculate radiation for the selected period.
Summarize radiation and rooftop area for each building.
Compare potential classes and inspect monthly patterns.
review: Review surface-model resolution, rooftop geometry and shadow assumptions.
Modeled radiation is a screening input; installation feasibility needs further assessment.

records.name: Urban Heat Risk Assessment
records.question: Where do heat exposure, population sensitivity and limited cooling capacity overlap?
records.summary: Build a heat-risk index for Jeddah using temperature history, land cover and population context.
overview: The Jeddah demonstration brings together Landsat surface-temperature history, ESA WorldCover and WorldPop. It describes checks on resolution, alignment and coordinate systems before the analytical layers are combined.

The index represents heat exposure, adaptive capacity and population sensitivity. Its mapped patterns support examination of heat-priority areas and discussion of measures such as shade, vegetation and reflective surfaces.
inputs: Surface-temperature observations and a defined historical period
Land cover describing built-up and vegetated areas
Population distribution and a common analysis grid
steps: Inspect the input periods, resolution and coordinate systems.
Develop temperature, land-cover and population indicators on a common grid.
Normalize and combine the indicators into the stated heat-risk index.
Map the index and examine priority clusters with local context.
outputs: Evidence to support review of possible mitigation locations
review: Distinguish land-surface temperature from direct human heat exposure.
Review indicator weights and population redistribution assumptions.
